meta.title: Who really said "Death solves all problems. No man, no problem"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Stalin. The line comes from Anatoly Rybakov's 1987 novel Children of the Arbat, where a fictional Stalin says it. No record shows Stalin said it.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Death solves all problems. No man, no problem'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Stalin: a line from Anatoly Rybakov's 1987 novel Children of the Arbat, put in the mouth of a fictional Stalin. Rybakov said he may have invented it.

answer.label: Not Joseph Stalin — actually Anatoly Rybakov
answer.sourceLine: The line comes from Rybakov’s novel Children of the Arbat (1987). There a fictional Stalin says «Смерть решает все проблемы. Нет человека, и нет проблемы» while talking about the shooting of military specialists at Tsaritsyn in 1918. No evidence shows the real Stalin ever said or wrote it, and Rybakov later said he may have “made it up myself.”

source.heading: Where the line actually comes from

docMeta.dd: 1987, in Russian, first as a serial
English translation by Harold Shukman (Little, Brown, 1988). We could not check the exact English wording of this line in that edition.

source.excerpt: «Смерть решает все проблемы. Нет человека, и нет проблемы.» — In English: “Death solves all problems. No man, no problem.”
trail: Wikiquote ↗ lists “Death solves all problems — no man, no problem” under Stalin’s Misattributed quotes. It says the line comes from Rybakov’s novel Children of the Arbat (1987), and that in a later memoir Rybakov admitted he had no source for it.

Serov’s Encyclopedic Dictionary of Winged Words and Expressions ↗ says the phrase is wrongly attributed to Stalin and that there is no evidence he ever said or wrote anything like it. It gives the novel’s wording and quotes Rybakov’s memoir Roman-vospominanie (1997): he “possibly heard it from someone, possibly made it up myself.”
Russian Wikiquote ↗ agrees. It says Stalin never said the phrase and that it first appeared in Rybakov’s Children of the Arbat, published in the summer of 1987.
Quote Investigator has not written about this quote. We found no speech, letter, or document by Stalin that contains it.
source.cutTag: Spoken by a character in a novel
source.excerptNote: The Russian wording comes from Serov’s dictionary of catchphrases ↗, which places it in a passage where the novel’s Stalin talks about the shooting of military specialists at Tsaritsyn in 1918. The English form is the one that circulates online. We have not checked it against Shukman’s printed translation.

source.rightsNote: The line was first published in Rybakov’s novel Children of the Arbat in 1987, and the English translation by Harold Shukman first appeared in 1988 (Wikipedia ↗). Both came out long after 1931, so the novel and its translation are presumed to be in copyright in the United States. A short quotation of a single line is commonly treated as fair use.

author.name: Anatoly Rybakov
author.heading: About the real author
author.metaLine: 1911–1998 · Soviet and Russian novelist, author of the Children of the Arbat trilogy
author.bio: Anatoly Naumovich Rybakov wrote the anti-Stalinist Children of the Arbat trilogy, the novel Heavy Sand, and popular children’s books such as Dirk and Bronze Bird. The NKVD arrested him in 1934 and exiled him to Siberia for three years. Children of the Arbat was suppressed for years and finally came out in 1987, during perestroika. It became a publishing sensation, largely because of its portrait of Stalin as a scheming, paranoid figure.

misattribution.heading: How it got pinned on Stalin
misattribution.intro: A novelist wrote the line for his fictional Stalin, and over time it lost the novel and kept the dictator.

items.why: Wikiquote ↗ files the line under Stalin’s misattributed quotes. Serov ↗ says there is no evidence he ever said or wrote anything like it. The words belong to the Stalin character in Rybakov’s novel.

On Goodreads’ reader-submitted quotes page for Harris’s thriller Archangel ↗, the line appears credited to “J. V. Stalin, 1918”. We have not checked it against the printed book. The year 1918 matches the Tsaritsyn episode the novel describes, which may explain why the line carries a date as if it were a historical remark.

items.who: «Есть человек — есть проблема, нет человека — нет проблемы»
items.why: The longer Russian saying (“There’s a person, there’s a problem; no person, no problem”) is also credited to Stalin. Both Serov ↗ and Russian Wikiquote ↗ trace it to Rybakov’s novel, not to Stalin.

misattribution.truthLine: The line is fiction: Anatoly Rybakov wrote it for the Stalin character in Children of the Arbat (1987), and by his own account he may have made it up himself ↗.

context.heading: Why a novel's line became a “Stalin quote”
lead: According to Wikipedia ↗, Rybakov wrote Children of the Arbat between 1966 and 1983, but it was suppressed until perestroika. When it was finally published in 1987 it became a sensation, in large part because of its unflattering portrait of Stalin. The short, brutal line Rybakov gave his Stalin sounded so much like the real man’s politics that readers began to quote it as his own words.

Rybakov never claimed it was a documented remark. According to Serov ↗, in his 1997 memoir he called it Stalin’s principle, summed up in a phrase of his own, and claimed a novelist’s right to do that. The sentiment may fit Stalin, but the sentence belongs to Rybakov.
context.pull: “That was Stalin’s principle. I simply formulated it briefly.” — Anatoly Rybakov, as quoted by Serov
